turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit, I'm Sister Naledi, I'll do your observations before the doctor comes in. Have a seat on the bed for me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Shame, thank you, I'm a bit of a mess. We were at my cousin Thandi's wedding in Stellenbosch on Saturday, and since Sunday morning I've basically lived in the loo.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Ag, shame. Arm out straight, the cuff's going on, try not to chat while it inflates.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, ja. I drove through from Rondebosch and got stuck at the robot by the N1, and then load shedding hit the complex so the fan was off all night.

[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one-oh-eight over seventy-two. Pulse is ninety-eight, temperature thirty-six point eight, oxygen ninety-eight percent, and you're breathing at sixteen. The doctor's just finishing next door.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety-eight high? I usually sit in the seventies when I'm well, though my watch has been dodgy since I dropped it at netball.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Naidoo, I've got Sister's numbers. Tell me what's been going on, and I'll jump in if I need to pin a detail.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Saturday we ate around seven, prawns, a creamy chicken, roast potatoes, malva pudding, the lot. I felt fine that night, just full, and Sunday morning around five I woke with cramps and had to run. Today's Wednesday, so this is day three, I counted it in the car.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Diarrhoea since Sunday morning, three days. Any vomiting, or just the runs?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Both. The vomiting started Sunday evening, three times that night and twice on Monday, and the last one was yesterday morning, Tuesday, just yellow fluid. It went on for about two days and then stopped, but the tummy is still going.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): How many times are you opening your bowels? Roughly is fine, I know counting falls apart.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish, I tried and then I gave up. Yesterday I stopped counting after the fourth, so maybe eight, could have been nine, I don't have a proper number. This morning I've already been four times and it's only half past ten.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood, or black stool?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No blood, and nothing black. I checked because my aunt once had blood and it turned into a whole saga. It's watery, brownish-yellow, and maybe a speck of mucus once but I wouldn't swear to that.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the mucus if you're not sure. Did anyone else from the wedding fall ill?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, my cousin Lerato WhatsApped that she's got the runs too, and two bridesmaids, and the groom's brother was vomiting in the parking lot. The bride herself is fine, which is lucky, shame.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): So a shared meal looks more likely than something you caught alone. What have you taken for it?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): My cousin in Joburg, she's a nurse, told me not to take Imodium for a wedding-food bug, let it come out. I was desperate to get to the car, so I bought loperamide at Clicks, the capsules say two milligrams. I took two capsules yesterday afternoon, that's four milligrams not two, I always mix that up, and one capsule this morning.

[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Two milligram capsules, two yesterday and one today. With a food-related gastro, loperamide can hold the irritant in the gut, so it isn't what I'd have chosen, and I'd like you to stop it.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, I knew it. Ja, I'll stop. I also used to take pantoprazole forty milligrams, one in the morning, for heartburn, and I stopped it in March because the heartburn had settled.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March, not taking it now. Anything else you were given that you actually swallowed?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Last winter the GP wrote ciprofloxacin for a bladder infection, but I never took it and I never even fetched it from the chemist. I drank water and cranberry juice and it passed, so that one doesn't count, hey?
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you never took it, it isn't your medicine, and we'll leave it out.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): This morning I nearly took my husband's metformin, the bottle was on the counter, five hundred milligrams, twice a day for his sugar. I didn't swallow any, it's his, he's the one with type two, not me.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): His metformin, not yours, I'm ignoring it completely. Any old blood results I should know about?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometime last year, I can't remember if it was August or October, they did a full blood count and said my haemoglobin was borderline, just under normal. They never gave me a number I still remember, just said eat more liver, which I tried once and, yoh, never again.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Borderline haemoglobin, no figure, and the date's fuzzy, so I won't treat that as a firm result today. Are you thirsty, dizzy, passing urine?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Very thirsty, and my mouth feels like cardboard even though I'm sipping water. When I stand up the room tilts for a second, not fainting, just woozy. The urine is dark yellow and small, maybe three times yesterday, and I kept mixing those up with the loo trips.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or shakes?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. Sunday night I felt flushed and the old thermometer read thirty-six point five, so not a fever, and I haven't been shivery today.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines or foods?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing, no drug allergies and no food allergies. My sister keeps pushing her biotin gummies on me for her hair, big bottle, but I've never taken them, they just taste like sweets.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): No allergies, and your sister's biotin stays hers. I'm going to examine you, and I'm expecting a soft tummy and some dryness if this is straightforward gastro. Say if I press too hard.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The cramps sit low across the bottom, left a bit more than the right, and they come in waves just before I have to go. I've also been exhausted, I could sleep at my desk, and I'm a grade four teacher so the kids would just take over.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mouth's dry, tongue a bit coated, lips dry. Tummy is soft, mild tenderness low on the left, no guarding and no rebound, so I'm not thinking of a surgical abdomen.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): It hurts when you press, but it's the same cramp, not a new sharp pain. Our grade fours have a reading assessment tomorrow and I hate the thought of a substitute who doesn't know the phonics programme.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, several people were ill after one wedding meal, you've had diarrhoea for three days, the vomiting has stopped, and you're dry. My working impression is acute gastroenteritis from that meal. It could be viral or it could be a bacterial toxin or a mild bacterial infection, and I can't separate those sitting here.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I need antibiotics? My neighbour got a three-day course for something similar and she was back at CrossFit, which is not my scene at all.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not now. No blood, no fever, soft tummy, so antibiotics would likely do more harm, and what you actually need is fluid. Stop the loperamide, and start oral rehydration salts, one sachet in two hundred mils of water, after each loose stool.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): One sachet, two hundred mils, after every time I go. I'll get it at Dis-Chem by the robot, they know me, I've been in twice this week for wet wipes already.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Small sips rather than big gulps, so you don't bring it back up. Bland food if you're hungry, toast, banana or rice, and skip the braai and the creamy sauces. Wash your hands well so you don't pass it to the grade fours.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, no braai. Should I do a stool test? I read online they can tell you the exact bug, and I know I shouldn't google, but I did, at two in the morning.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the diarrhoea hasn't settled in two days, we might send a stool sample. I'm not ordering it today, most of these settle and a sample now rarely changes the plan.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): What about a scan? Lerato's GP sent her for one years ago for a tummy thing and it was nothing, just wind, she still talks about the gel being cold.

[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): We might do a scan if it does not settle, an ultrasound of the abdomen, only if you're still bad or the pain changes, not today. Come back if it has not settled in two weeks.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): If it hasn't settled in two weeks, I come back. What if I can't keep the sips down before that, or I see blood?
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then you don't wait. If you can't keep fluids down, if there's blood, if you faint, or if a fever starts, come in the same day, casualty if we're shut.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the wooziness just the dryness? It happens when I get up off the couch, and that couch is ancient, from my husband's varsity flat, he refuses to replace it.

[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, light-headed on standing fits with being mildly dehydrated, not a heart problem from what I see. Your pressure is fine and the pulse is only a touch quick, which matches that.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): I can give her two sachets from the cupboard, Doctor, so she isn't stuck if Dis-Chem's queue is out the door.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please do, Sister. Same mixing, one sachet in two hundred mils, and she can buy the rest.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks, Sister. Must I stay off tomorrow? Leaving the reading assessment with a sub who doesn't know our programme stresses me more than the tummy, almost.

[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stay home tomorrow, you're still infectious while it's this frequent, and you need a loo nearby. If by Friday it's down to a couple of soft stools and you're keeping fluids, you can go back, and if not, stay off.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): One more thing, I've got Buscopan at home, hyoscine, ten milligrams, but I haven't taken any this week, I wasn't sure with the Imodium. There's also a half box of my sister's biotin still on the counter but that's hers, as I said.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): You haven't taken the hyoscine, so it doesn't go on your list, and I wouldn't start it for this. Don't restart the pantoprazole either. Fluids are the treatment.

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp. Stop the Imodium, none of my husband's pills, rehydration after each loose stool, home tomorrow, back if it hasn't settled in two weeks, sooner if I can't drink or I see blood. Sorry I went on, I always do when I'm nervous, even about the couch.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): You did fine. Rest, sip, and Sister will see you out with those sachets.

spec.situation: Diarrhoea and vomiting after a trip or a wedding meal; others at the event are ill; patient counts bowel movements loosely; takes loperamide against advice; mild dehydration signs; stool test conditional; advice on fluids.
features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

bad.reason: Full blood count was done, but not requested by patient; who requested it is unstated.
